correctness.rationale: The published \(b=c\) GC2 inequality is specialized exactly to \(a=2b\), then transformed using \(t=|\cos x|\). Positivity restricts \(t\) to \((0,1/4)\); the coupling sign forces one flank; the inequality is exactly \(F(t)<|\eta b|<G(t)\). Explicit derivatives show \(F\) and \(G\) strictly decrease to the common threshold \(\sqrt{5/3}(x_m-\varepsilon\arcsin(1/4))\), so each eligible \(m\) contributes exactly one connected interval and the ceiling formula counts them.

evidence: Exner--Turek 2014 condition (19) is the exact GC2 inequality for \(b=c\); Corollary 4.5(i) proves only finitely many GC2-generated gaps for rational \(a/b\).
Theorem 4.1(i) of the same paper proves infinitely many GC1 gaps for rational \(a/b\) and nonzero coupling, so the new count cannot be misread as a total-gap count.
Exner--Turek 2017 constructs rectangular-lattice examples with prescribed exact finite total gap counts using suitable irrational edge ratios, a different geometry and regime.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The source theorem covers the general family qualitatively, while the present statement resolves the complete GC2 component count only for the natural \(2:1:1\) commensurate specialization.

originality.rationale: The accepted claim is only the exact GC2 threshold and count law for the \(2:1:1\) commensurate honeycomb. The source condition, its rational-ratio finiteness result, and rational GC1 infinitude are credited; later prescribed-gap work concerns rectangular lattices with irrational ratios.

value.rationale: The result is a complete classification across all coupling strengths for a natural one-parameter specialization, with exact birth thresholds, sign-dependent locations, and an explicit count formula.
